<explanation>
Based on both the file tree and the README, XPipe is a desktop-based, modular shell connection hub and remote file management application. Its primary purpose is to serve as an integrated “front door” to a wide variety of remote systems—via SSH, containers (Docker, Podman, LXD/incus), virtualization platforms (Proxmox, Hyper-V, KVM, VMware), Windows remote sessions, Kubernetes clusters, and even tunneling/secure vault features. It is built in Java and organized into multiple Gradle subprojects that separate core application logic, beacon communications, extensions, and additional functionality.

Below is a detailed explanation and guideline for drawing the system design diagram tailored for XPipe:

1. Identify the Main Components:
   • User Interface (UI) Module: This is the presentation layer offering multiple views:
       – Connection hub view (organized hierarchical list of remote connections).
       – Remote file browser view.
       – Terminal launcher view.
       – Scripting and vault management UI.
   • Core Application Module: Located primarily in the “app” and “core” folders, this layer handles:
       – Application bootstrap, configuration, and lifecycle.
       – Connection management logic (processing and orchestrating different connection types).
       – File system interactions and remote actions.
       – Internationalization (lang) and resource handling.
   • Beacon/Communication Module: This subproject (found in the “beacon” directory) seems responsible for:
       – Establishing two-way communication between XPipe and remote endpoints.
       – Handling various exchange protocols (for file system actions, shell session commands, authentication exchanges, etc.).
   • Extension / Plugin System: XPipe is designed to be extensible and modular. The “ext” directory (with several subprojects like ext/base, ext/proc, ext/system, ext/uacc) contains:
       – Additional actions, browser integrations, desktop integrations.
       – Custom connection types and enhanced services that plug into the core.
   • API Layer: XPipe exposes programmatic access via an HTTP API (documented in the OpenAPI spec). This component manages:
       – The API endpoint component that allows external tooling (or even the internal extension system) to control XPipe programmatically.
   • External Integration Layer: Represented as the various connection protocols (SSH, Docker, Kubernetes, etc.) that XPipe supports. This can be visualized as a set of “external services” which the core and its extensions integrate with.

2. Relationships and Interactions:
   • The UI layer interacts with the core application logic to launch terminal sessions, manage file transfers, and authenticate vault operations.
   • The Core module acts as the brain, coordinating authentication, configuration, and invoking the right extension or beacon exchange for the requested remote connection.
   • When a connection is requested (say, an SSH or container session), the core will trigger the appropriate extension (from ext/base, ext/system, …) and possibly consult the beacon module to manage low-level protocol exchanges.
   • The API layer serves as an alternate path for commanding operations, allowing both UI components and external REST clients to manage connections and scripting functionalities.
   • The extension framework is designed for modularity: new protocols or actions are implemented as separate modules (e.g., handling Incus, LXD, Podman, etc.) and plugged into the system during runtime.

3. Architectural Patterns and Design Principles:
   • Modular Design – Each major feature is clearly separated into its own module (app, beacon, core, ext/…).
   • Layered Architecture – Presentation (UI) is separated from business logic (core) and from communication (beacon) and integration points (extensions).
   • Extensibility – A plugin/extension system allows the addition of new connection types and custom commands.
   • Loose coupling – The API and beacon modules encapsulate low-level details and communicate with the core via clearly defined interfaces.
   • Separation of concerns – Each directory (for example, “app” handles main application logic and UI, “core” manages lower-level file operations and process management, “ext” handles custom actions) reinforces clean boundaries.

4. Technologies, Frameworks, and Libraries:
   • Java (with modularization, as seen by the presence of module-info.java files).
   • Gradle as the build and dependency management tool.
   • UI resources (CSS, images, icons) in the “app/src/main/resources” directory.
   • Various external libraries bundled under “lib” and via Gradle scripts, such as Jackson (for JSON), and others (possibly for SSH and process control).
   • OpenAPI spec (openapi.yaml) for the API layer.

5. Guidelines for Tailoring the Diagram:
   • For a full-stack-like desktop application, clearly separate:
         – The Presentation Layer (UI components for connection hub, file browser, terminal)
         – The Business/Logic Layer (core connection processing, file management, session management)
         – The Integration/Extension Layer (beacon services and extension plugins managing protocol-specific tasks)
   • Depict how the user initiates actions from the UI, leading the core to invoke extensions and eventually interact with remote services.
   • Highlight the role of the secure vault and scripting system as specialized modules that provide security and automation features.

6. Essential Elements in the Diagram:
   • Label each module/component clearly; use boxes/shapes to encapsulate:
         – “User Interface” (with sub-components for connections hub, browser, terminal, scripting, and vault)
         – “Core Application Logic” (with connection management, process handling, configuration, and localization)
         – “Beacon Communication Module” (handling protocol exchanges and session orchestration)
         – “Extensions/Plugins” (with subdivisions for base actions, system integrations, processing, etc.)
         – “API Server” (HTTP interface for programmatic control)
         – “External Systems” (SSH servers, container engines, VMs, Kubernetes clusters, etc.)
   • Use directional arrows to illustrate data flows and dependencies. For example:
         – An arrow from the “User Interface” to the “Core Application Logic”.
         – From “Core Application Logic” to “Beacon Module” and to various “Extension Modules”.
         – Arrows from the “Extensions” and “Core” to “External Systems”.
         – Arrows from the “API Server” to the “Core” and vice versa.
   • Employ color coding or distinct shapes to differentiate layers (presentation, business logic, integration, external systems).

When drawing the diagram, start with the user at the top (or left), followed by the core logic layer, then the extension/communication modules, and finally the remote/external systems. This layered view will reflect the separation of concerns and make it easier to understand data flow, dependencies, and the extensible nature of XPipe.

Overall, be detailed in capturing each component and their interactions, ensuring that the diagram covers the modular architecture (with submodules such as app, core, beacon, and ext) and provides a clear overview of how user actions are translated into remote operations through the orchestrated interaction of these components.

This should give you a comprehensive, accurate, and highly detailed system design diagram tailored specifically for XPipe’s purpose and structure.
</explanation>
